newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS - Caracas stocks record rise not all good news.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Caracas stocks record rise not all good news.

text.p: Even a near vertical boom in the Venezuelan stock market has its downside.

Heavy foreign bidding has taken Latin America's best performing stock market 57 percent ahead in dollar terms so far this year in a trend -- occasional profit-taking aside -- local brokers only see continuing.
"But the mania presents a challenge to Venezuelan officials who are trying to keep macro-restructuring on track," said New York-based IDEA in a market comment.

Last week alone the market's 19-share index rose eight percent as foreign investors -- egged-on by expectations of local telephone company CANTV's slated November share offering -- placed an estimated $20-50 million every day in a bourse whose average turnover usually floats below the $5 million mark.

"Foreign funds have upped their Venezuela weighting so I think we'll see rises until the end of the year," said Merinvest analyst Boris Molina. And on Monday foreign bids edged the market ahead again to its seventh consecutive record high as the index closed at 5,481.90.
It's those foreign capital inflows that have put the Central Bank in a bind, IDEA argues.

Because of them, the Bank can either maintain its foreign exchange target or its inflation target -- but not both. And without some very skilled macro-economic management, "Venezuela risks a liquidity blow-out in both financial markets and its targets," warned IDEA.

On the one hand, the Central Bank can focus its energies on depreciating an increasingly over-valued bolivar. The need to do so was underlined last week when the unit firmed a startling 0.8 percent to close at 472 against the dollar.
That move took local traders by surprise, not least because it flew in the opposite direction of Venezuela's 500 bolivar per dollar year-end target.

But while the Central Bank could inject more liquidity into local markets, so producing a weaker bolivar, that would also jeopardize what Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff recently admitted was already an unlikely 1.5 percent December inflation target. August inflation stood at 4.1 percent.

Alternatively, the Central Bank could forsake its foreign exchange target and focus instead on bringing down inflation by mopping-up liquidity through more local debt issues, so increasing interest rates, IDEA said.

Then, however, higher interest rates would prompt greater foreign capital inflows, so making the bolivar appreciate and exacerbating the original problem. The cost of financing government debt would also rise -- so enlarging the fiscal deficit.
Faced with such a bind, "the usual prescription is to cut government spending," says IDEA.
But long-flouted Venezuelan plans to restructure public services and shrink the state are yet to materialize.

And while an estimated $2.5 billion-plus windfall from recent international oil price rises has been earmarked for a special off-budget fund, "it's very hard to sell spending cuts precisely because you have too much money," said local CNI consultant Frank Amador.

With over $1.5 billion in government credits pending approval when Congress reconvenes in October, "Venezuelan officials have shown the opposite inclination...and risk a liquidity blow-out," said IDEA.
